title: Calculus 2
semester: 15-week semester · 12 instructional units · Week 15 review and assessment
description: A coherent second-semester calculus pathway through integration techniques, applications, differential equations, infinite series, and introductory parametric and polar calculus.
outcomes: Interpret definite integrals through accumulation and Riemann sums, and apply both parts of the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus.
Select and carry out appropriate integration techniques, including substitution, parts, trigonometric methods, and partial fractions.
Model geometric and physical quantities with definite integrals while attending to orientation, domains, and dimensional units.
Solve separable differential equations with initial conditions and interpret exponential, cooling, logistic, and mixing models.
Analyze improper integrals, sequences, and numerical series using limits, comparisons, and standard convergence tests.
Construct and use power and Taylor series, then extend derivative and area ideas to parametric and polar curves.

units.title: Riemann Sums, Definite Integrals, and the FTC
units.summary: Build the definite integral from partition width, sample points, and limiting Riemann sums, emphasizing that it measures net signed accumulation rather than automatically giving geometric area. Connect evaluation by antiderivatives with both parts of the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, checking endpoints carefully and differentiating accumulation functions with the chain rule when an upper limit varies.
objectives: Compute left and right Riemann sums from a specified interval, partition, and sampling rule.
Evaluate definite integrals by applying an antiderivative at both endpoints with correct subtraction.
Differentiate accumulation functions using the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus and account for variable limits.

units.title: Integration by Substitution
units.summary: Recognize an inner expression whose differential is present up to a constant factor, then rewrite the entire integral in one temporary variable. For indefinite integrals return to the original variable; for definite integrals either transform both bounds or return to the original antiderivative before evaluation, and watch for reversed differentials, missing constant factors, and logarithm domains.
objectives: Choose substitutions that align an inner expression with its differential, including constant correction factors.
Find indefinite integrals by substitution and rewrite the antiderivative in the original variable.
Evaluate definite integrals by substitution while transforming the limits consistently.

units.title: Integration by Parts
units.summary: Derive integration by parts from the product rule and choose u and dv so the new integral is simpler, using logarithmic, inverse-trigonometric, algebraic, trigonometric, and exponential factors as a guide. Track every minus sign and coefficient through repeated parts, and recognize cyclic cases where the original integral returns and must be solved algebraically.
objectives: Select u and dv strategically and apply the integration-by-parts formula with consistent signs.
Evaluate integrals requiring repeated parts, including products with higher-degree polynomial factors.
Resolve cyclic integration-by-parts problems involving paired exponential and trigonometric factors.

units.title: Trigonometric Integrals and Powers
units.summary: Use Pythagorean identities and parity to integrate products and powers of sine, cosine, tangent, and secant, saving one factor for the differential when an odd power permits. For even sine or cosine powers use half-angle identities; for tangent and secant retain suitable secant-squared or secant-tangent factors, and distinguish these patterns before attempting substitution.
objectives: Integrate odd powers of sine or cosine by saving one factor and converting the remaining even power.
Apply half-angle identities to even powers without losing factor-of-two coefficients.
Integrate standard secant-tangent powers by pairing identities with an appropriate differential.

units.title: Trigonometric Substitution
units.summary: Match radicals and quadratic denominators to substitutions based on sine, tangent, or secant, using a reference triangle and the corresponding Pythagorean identity. Convert the differential as well as the integrand, respect domain branches when simplifying square roots, and back-substitute into a function of x rather than leaving the final antiderivative in the angle variable.
objectives: Identify appropriate trigonometric substitutions for sums and differences of squares.
Transform the differential and simplify radical factors using identities on a stated domain.
Back-substitute to express antiderivatives in the original variable and verify domain-sensitive factors.

units.title: Partial Fractions
units.summary: Prepare rational integrands by using long division when the numerator degree is at least the denominator degree, then factor the denominator completely over the real numbers. Set up distinct linear, repeated linear, and irreducible quadratic terms correctly; integrate logarithmic terms with domain awareness and inverse-tangent terms with the coefficient produced by completing the square.
objectives: Decompose rational functions with distinct or repeated linear factors and determine all coefficients.
Handle irreducible quadratic denominators by completing the square when needed.
Use polynomial long division before decomposition for improper rational functions.

units.title: Improper Integrals and Comparison
units.summary: Replace an infinite endpoint or an interior singular endpoint with a finite parameter and take the appropriate one-sided limit only after integrating. Distinguish convergence of a finite limiting value from boundedness alone at a finite cutoff; comparison with a convergent dominant integrand or a divergent smaller nonnegative integrand can settle behavior without finding the original value.
objectives: Evaluate convergent Type 1 and Type 2 improper integrals through finite-cutoff limits.
Identify finite power thresholds for standard infinite-interval and endpoint-singularity integrals.
Apply direct comparison to nonnegative integrands and evaluate finite comparison bounds accurately.

units.title: Areas Between Curves and Arc Length
units.summary: Determine intersections and choose vertical or horizontal slices before integrating upper minus lower or right minus left expressions; split the interval whenever that ordering changes. Keep total area distinct from net signed integral by integrating absolute height across sign changes, and compute arc length from a square-root integral of one plus the squared derivative when that derivative is integrable on the interval.
objectives: Find intersection points and set up areas using either vertical or horizontal slices.
Compute total area when curves cross or the boundary lies across the axis rather than relying on signed area.
Evaluate arc length with the square-root formula and simplify perfect-square radicands on their domains.

units.title: Volumes by Disks, Washers, and Shells; Work
units.summary: Sketch the generating region and axis of rotation before deciding whether cross-sections or cylindrical shells give the simpler integral, identifying outer and inner radii or shell radius and height in the integration variable. Apply the same accumulation idea to work as force times small displacement, using spring or variable-force laws and reporting numerical work in the units stated by the model.
objectives: Set up disk and washer integrals with cross-sections perpendicular to an axis of rotation.
Set up shell integrals with radius, height, and thickness expressed in one consistent variable.
Calculate work from Hooke's law or a variable force and distinguish its units from volume.

units.title: Separable Differential Equations and Applications
units.summary: Separate variables only after preserving constant and equilibrium solutions, integrate both sides with a single combined constant, and use an initial condition before evaluating a requested quantity. Interpret exponential growth and decay, Newton cooling, logistic change, and mixing through their rates and limiting states, checking that signs, domains, and initial values agree with the selected solution branch.
objectives: Solve separable initial-value problems and select the solution branch consistent with the initial condition.
Use exponential and Newton cooling laws to evaluate modeled quantities at specified times.
Analyze logistic and mixing models algebraically after separation and verify physically sensible values.

units.title: Sequences and Numerical Series
units.summary: Distinguish convergence of a sequence of terms from convergence of its series of partial sums, beginning with the divergence test but never treating a zero term limit as proof of convergence. Develop geometric and telescoping sums, p-series, integral and comparison tests, alternating error control, ratio and root tests, and absolute versus conditional convergence, always asking for finite limits, partial sums, thresholds, or error bounds.
objectives: Evaluate sequence limits using algebraic simplification and distinguish them from series sums.
Compute geometric, finite partial, and telescoping sums while tracking starting indices.
Choose and apply divergence, integral, comparison, alternating, ratio, and root tests appropriately.
Classify absolute and conditional convergence through separate analysis of signed and absolute series.

units.title: Power and Taylor Series; Parametric and Polar Preview
units.summary: Find power-series centers and radii with ratio or root limits, then test endpoints separately because the radius alone never decides endpoint behavior; represent functions through Taylor coefficients and polynomial approximations. Close with parametric slopes and arc length from derivatives with respect to the parameter, and polar slopes and sector area from products and one-half r squared, previewing how integral ideas transfer to new coordinates.
objectives: Determine a power series radius of convergence and examine endpoint behavior with separate numerical series.
Compute Taylor coefficients and evaluate finite Taylor polynomials for representation and approximation.
Calculate parametric derivatives and arc lengths from parameter derivatives without eliminating the parameter.
Evaluate elementary polar slopes and sector areas while respecting angular domains and factors of one-half.
